subject: biology

items.q: A student is given the names of two organisms: Panthera leo and Panthera pardus. Which Linnaean group is given by the shared name Panthera?
items.correct: Their genus in the Linnaean system
items.misconception: Their order in the Linnaean system
items.why: Students remember that the two-part name places an organism in the Linnaean groups, but kingdom, phylum, class, order and family are more familiar words than genus, and 'family' sounds like a group of close relatives. Organisms are named by the binomial system of genus and species. The first part of the name gives the genus and the second part gives the species; family and order are separate, larger Linnaean groups.
items.random_wrong: Their family in the Linnaean system

items.q: Linnaeus classified living things depending on their structure and characteristics. Why were new models of classification later proposed?
items.correct: Because improved microscopes showed internal structures
items.misconception: Because much larger numbers of species were discovered
items.why: Students think a classification system only has to change when there are more organisms to fit into it, rather than when new evidence about the organisms themselves becomes available. As evidence of internal structures became more developed due to improvements in microscopes, and the understanding of biochemical processes progressed, new models of classification were proposed.
items.random_wrong: Because fossils of many extinct organisms were discovered

items.q: In the three-domain system developed by Carl Woese, into which three groups are organisms divided?
items.why: Archaea are described as primitive bacteria and look similar to bacteria, so students treat the two as one group and do not realise the domains were separated using different evidence. Due to evidence available from chemical analysis, the three-domain system developed by Carl Woese divides organisms into Archaea (primitive bacteria usually living in extreme environments), Bacteria (true bacteria) and Eukaryota.

items.q: In the binomial name Panthera leo, which part gives the species?
items.correct: The second part, leo, gives the species.
items.misconception: The first part of a binomial name gives the species and the second part gives the genus.
items.why: Students learn that the name is made of a genus and a species but not which comes first, and they assume the part shared by several organisms must be the species because a species is the group they meet most often. Organisms are named by the binomial system of genus and species, in that order: in Panthera leo the genus is Panthera and the species is leo.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which data do scientists use to draw an evolutionary tree?
items.correct: Current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.
items.misconception: Evolutionary trees are drawn using fossil data only.
items.why: Evolutionary trees are usually met alongside work on fossils and extinction, so students assume every organism on the tree has been placed there using fossil evidence. Evolutionary trees are a method used by scientists to show how they believe organisms are related. They use current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which organisms are included in the domain Eukaryota?
items.correct: Protists, fungi, plants and animals are all included in Eukaryota.
items.misconception: Protists, fungi, plants and animals are each a separate domain of their own.
items.why: Students have already met these as separate groups of organisms and assume the three-domain system simply renames those groups, so they list them alongside Archaea and Bacteria. In the three-domain system organisms are divided into Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota; Eukaryota is the domain which includes protists, fungi, plants and animals.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Biology (8461) specification; section 4.6.4 Classification of Living Organisms
